newsitem.title: USA: Strikes at GM to cost automaker $490 million in Q2.
newsitem.headline: Strikes at GM to cost automaker $490 million in Q2.

text.p: While bargainers worked to end a 69-day strike at General Motors Corp., the automaker disclosed Monday that work stoppages have taken a $490 million bite out of its second-quarter profits.

GM said in a U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission filing it has lost 96,000 units of production because of the continuing strike at its Pontiac, Mich., full-size truck plant and an earlier strike at its Oklahoma City passenger car plant.
Including the $1.2 billion GM lost from strikes in the United States and Canada last year, labor strife has cost the world's largest automaker $1.69 billion since the beginning of 1996.

The second-quarter earnings impact is equal to 67 cents a a share on an after-tax basis. Based on the consensus analyst net earnings estimate of $2.04 billion when the second quarter began, Burnham Securities Inc. analyst David Healy said the strikes will bring GM's second-quarter net income down to about $1.5 billion.

GM said in the filing it is "likely" to recover some of the lost units through increased truck production in the future. The $490 million consists of losses to date of $375 million from its North American Operations; $85 million from its Delphi Automotive Systems; and $30 million from the Delco Electronics unit of Hughes Electronics Corp..
The strike in Oklahoma City, where GM produces its new Chevrolet Malibu and Oldsmobile Cutlass sedans, started April 4 and ended May 27.
United Auto Worker union and company bargainers talked all night Sunday and continued to negotiate Monday to resolve the Pontiac work stoppage, said Jim Abare, sourcing coordinator for UAW Local 594.

Abare said union officials are "cautiously optimistic" about a settlement. About 5,800 hourly workers at GM's Pontiac East truck assembly plant and nearby engineering and development facilty walked off the job April 22 in a dispute over a new three-year contract.
"We're negotiating and ready to settle this thing as soon as GM is serious and willing to get down to it," he said.

The talks include members of the UAW's international bargaining team, said Abare. Staffing continues to be a big sticking point. Also unresolved is when production could resume at the plant. GM's plants closed Monday for the annual two-week summer shutdown.

GM has resisted union demands to add more workers at the plant to ease overtime burdens. The Pontiac East facility is the lead plant for GM's next-generation full-size pickup. The company says efficiency gains will mean it needs 30 percent fewer workers to assemble the vehicles.
